blocks.title: Turn bytes into validated domain values
paragraphs: File handling has several independent responsibilities: acquire a resource, decode characters, parse records, validate fields, construct objects, process them and format output. A failure policy belongs at each boundary.

blocks.title: Read complete lines and keep parsing testable
paragraphs: This original station-count format is name|nonnegative-count, one record per line. The parser below owns no file handle: it accepts a Reader supplied by its caller, rejects malformed lines with a line number, and returns no partial result when a row fails. A caller can use a StringReader in tests.

BufferedReader reads text efficiently and readLine returns null at end-of-file. An empty line is a line, not EOF. Validate field count before indexing; preserve trailing empties; convert numbers and reject values outside the stated domain. Do not assume every course task allows malformed rows to be silently skipped.

blocks.title: Specify output and error behavior
paragraphs: Use a Writer for characters and define separators, order and line endings in the requirement. This report writes exactly name=count followed by a newline for each row, preserving list order. An empty list produces an empty report.

The method accepts a caller-owned Writer and propagates IOException. It does not claim that writing to a buffer guarantees bytes survived device failure. File writers must eventually be closed; flush sends buffered data onward but does not replace resource ownership.

blocks.title: The code that opens a resource normally closes it
paragraphs: At the application boundary, open your file Reader/Writer in try-with-resources. Successfully initialized resources are closed when the block exits normally or exceptionally. A parser accepting a caller-owned Reader should document that it leaves closure to the caller; closing System.in from a helper can disable later interaction.

Propagate I/O errors or translate them at a boundary that can explain the failure. Do not return an empty successful report merely because a file was unreadable. Test malformed content with an in-memory Reader and simulate read/write failures separately from valid empty input.

Writing directly to an output file can leave partial output if writing fails. This example does not promise atomic file replacement. An assignment that needs all-or-nothing output must state and design that additional requirement.

blocks.title: Keep parsing, processing and ownership separate
paragraphs: A good importer states its grammar, validation policy, resource owner and observable failures. Test content rules with in-memory I/O, then verify the real file boundary and its cleanup separately.

cards.prompt: What distinguishes a blank line from end-of-file in BufferedReader.readLine()?
cards.answer: A blank line returns an empty String. End-of-file returns null. A parser must handle blank rows using its declared format policy.

cards.prompt: Why test file-to-model parsing with a StringReader?
cards.answer: It supplies exact valid or malformed text without filesystem setup. The parser can be checked independently from opening files, permissions and UI reporting.

cards.prompt: Which details belong in an output-format test?
cards.answer: Field order, separators, record order, required line endings, empty output and any stated escaping. Assert required behavior, not an unrelated generated toString representation.

cards.prompt: If writing throws halfway through a report, is the output necessarily unchanged?
cards.answer: No. Some output may already have been written. Propagate the failure; only an explicitly designed atomic replacement scheme can promise all-or-nothing file output.

cards.prompt: Should a reusable parser always close the Reader passed to it?
cards.answer: Not without an ownership contract. Usually the caller that opens a resource closes it; a parser can leave a borrowed Reader open so the caller controls its lifetime.

cards.prompt: What does try-with-resources add on an exception path?
cards.answer: It closes successfully initialized AutoCloseable resources as the block exits, including when parsing or processing throws. It does not convert a failed operation into success.

guided.title: Design a failure-aware importer
guided.prompt: A studio imports rows token|quantity where quantity is an integer ≥0. Blank rows and malformed rows reject the entire import. The caller opens the file, and the processor consumes only a fully parsed list. Plan the parser, output and tests.

fields.label: Valid and malformed examples with expected outcomes
Output assertions and injected I/O failures

rubric: EOF and blank rows have different behavior.
A malformed later row does not return a successful partial list.
Caller-owned resources remain caller-owned, and file boundaries use try-with-resources.
Tests cover empty file, valid zero, missing field, negative/noninteger count, multirow failure and I/O errors.
reference: Use readLine until null, validate exactly two fields and nonnegative numeric content, and attach the failing line number. Accumulate locally and return only after all rows parse.
Test formatting separately with StringWriter. Use a throwing Reader/Writer for failure paths; the app reports the error and must not label the import saved or complete.
